claim: The caudal prelimbic area (PL), rostral part of the anterior cingulate area (ACA), medial visual area (VISm), and the ventral part of retrosplenial area (RSPv) form a highly interconnected circuit that presents a differential increase in Fos expression in response to predator exposure.
source: Thus, the caudal prelimbic area (PL), rostral part of the anterior cingulate area (ACA), medial visual area (VISm), and the ventral part of retrosplenial area (RSPv) form a highly interconnected circuit that presents a differential increase in Fos expression in response to predator exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019 study.

claim: Cytotoxic lesions of the elements of the cortical circuit had no impact on innate fear responses during predator exposure but had a profound impact on contextual fear memory.
source: Cytotoxic lesions of the elements of this cortical circuit apparently had no impact on innate fear responses during predator exposure but had a profound impact on contextual fear memory largely disrupting learned contextual fear responses in a predator-related environment (de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019 study.

claim: Lesions in the ACA had a larger impact on decreasing learned contextual fear responses versus lesions of the other elements of the cortical network.
source: Importantly, lesions in the ACA had a larger impact on decreasing learned contextual fear responses versus lesions of the other elements of this cortical network (de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019 study.

claim: The ACA seems to be necessary for the acquisition of contextual fear.
source: The ACA seems to be necessary for the acquisition of contextual fear. Pretraining inactivation of the ACA blocked fear acquisition (Tang et al., 2005; Bissière et al., 2008), and pretraining activation of the ACA using a mGluR agonist (Bissière et al., 2008) enhanced fear learning thus suggesting an involvement of the ACA in the acquisition of fear responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2005 and Bissière et al., 2008 studies.

claim: Pretraining inactivation of the ACA blocked fear acquisition.
source: Pretraining inactivation of the ACA blocked fear acquisition (Tang et al., 2005; Bissière et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2005 and Bissière et al., 2008 studies.

claim: Pretraining activation of the ACA using a mGluR agonist enhanced fear learning.
source: pretraining activation of the ACA using a mGluR agonist (Bissière et al., 2008) enhanced fear learning
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bissière et al., 2008 study.

claim: The insertion of an empty temporal gap between the CS and UCS makes learning the association critically dependent on the prefrontal cortex.
source: Of relevance, the insertion of an empty temporal gap, or trace, between the CS and UCS makes learning the association critically dependent on the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gilmartin et al., 2014 study.

claim: Recording studies in trace fear conditioning revealed units called 'bridging cells' in the prefrontal cortex that maintain firing during the trace intervals.
source: Recording studies in trace fear conditioning revealed units called "bridging cells" in the prefrontal cortex that maintain firing during the trace intervals, perhaps reflecting the maintenance of attentional resources during the CS-USC interval (Gilmartin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gilmartin et al., 2014 study.

claim: The ACA is required for memory consolidation.
source: The ACA is also required for memory consolidation. Infusion of the protein-synthesis inhibitor anisomycin in the ACA impairs memory consolidation of recent and remote memory (Einarsson and Nader, 2012), and virally mediated disruption of learning-induced dendritic spine growth in the ACA impairs memory consolidation (Vetere et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Einarsson and Nader, 2012 and Vetere et al., 2011 studies.

claim: Infusion of the protein-synthesis inhibitor anisomycin in the ACA impairs memory consolidation of recent and remote memory.
source: Infusion of the protein-synthesis inhibitor anisomycin in the ACA impairs memory consolidation of recent and remote memory (Einarsson and Nader, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Einarsson and Nader, 2012 study.

claim: Virally mediated disruption of learning-induced dendritic spine growth in the ACA impairs memory consolidation.
source: virally mediated disruption of learning-induced dendritic spine growth in the ACA impairs memory consolidation (Vetere et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vetere et al., 2011 study.

claim: The ACA has been largely associated with the encoding and retrieval of contextual fear memory at remote time points.
source: In fact, the ACA has been largely associated with the encoding and retrieval of contextual fear memory at remote time points (Frankland et al., 2004; Kitamura et al., 2017; Abate et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frankland et al., 2004, Kitamura et al., 2017, and Abate et al., 2018 studies.

claim: Pharmacogenetic silencing of the ACA during exposure to the predator did not change innate responses but significantly reduced contextual fear responses.
source: The results showed that compared to the control group, animals expressing Gi-coupled hM4Di treated before the cat exposure did not change innate responses but significantly reduced contextual fear responses (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B showing behavioral measurements.

claim: CNO treatment before the exposure to the predatory context significantly reduced risk assessment and increased exploration in animals injected with virus expressing Gi-coupled hM4Di.
source: Likewise, CNO treatment before the exposure to the predatory context also significantly reduced risk assessment and increased exploration in animals injected with virus expressing Gi-coupled hM4Di (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Silencing the ACA does not influence innate fear responses but affects both the acquisition and the expression of contextual fear to predator threat.
source: The results suggest that silencing the ACA does not influence innate fear responses but affects both the acquisition and the expression of contextual fear to predator threat.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of ACA silencing on contextual but not innate fear responses.

claim: During the cat exposure, the ventral retrosplenial (RSPv) and anteromedial visual (VISam) areas presented the largest percentage of FG retrogradely labeled cells expressing Fos (around 50% of the retrogradely labeled cells).
source: During the cat exposure, among the cortical inputs, the ventral retrosplenial (RSPv) and anteromedial visual (VISam) areas presented the largest percentage of FG retrogradely labeled cells expressing Fos (around 50% of the retrogradely labeled cells); the other cortical inputs to the ACA, including the medial orbital (ORBm) and prelimbic (PL) areas, displayed close to 30% of double-labeled cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: During cat exposure, a particularly large percentage of FG/Fos double-labeled cells were found in the central lateral (CL) and ventral anteromedial thalamic (AMv) nuclei—both of these contained more than 50% retrogradely labeled expressing Fos protein.
source: In addition, during cat exposure, a particularly large percentage of FG/Fos double-labeled cells were found in the central lateral (CL) and ventral anteromedial thalamic (AMv) nuclei—both of these contained more than 50% retrogradely labeled expressing Fos protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The CL and AMv are likely to convey information regarding the predatory threat.
source: Notably, the CL and AMv are likely to convey information regarding the predatory threat (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the activation patterns and anatomical connections discussed in the manuscript.

claim: During cat exposure, inputs to the ACA from the basolateral amygdalar nucleus, ventral hippocampus, lateral entorhinal area, and claustrum presented 25–30% FG/FOS double-labeled cells.
source: We also found that, during cat exposure, inputs to the ACA from the basolateral amygdalar nucleus, ventral hippocampus, lateral entorhinal area, and claustrum presented 25–30% FG/FOS double-labeled cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: During exposure to the predatory context, all cortical inputs to the ACA as well as the inputs from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and lateral entorhinal area presented close to 20–30% of FG-labeled cells expressing Fos protein.
source: Thus, during exposure to the predatory context, all cortical inputs to the ACA as well as the inputs from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and lateral entorhinal area presented close to 20–30% of FG-labeled cells expressing Fos protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: In the thalamus, the AMv displayed a relatively low percentage of double-labeled cells (close to 20%) during exposure to the predatory context.
source: In the thalamus, the AMv displayed a relatively low percentage of double-labeled cells (close to 20%), whereas the CL nucleus contained close to 40% of the retrogradely labeled cells expressing Fos protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The CL nucleus contained close to 40% of the retrogradely labeled cells expressing Fos protein during exposure to the predatory context.
source: In the thalamus, the AMv displayed a relatively low percentage of double-labeled cells (close to 20%), whereas the CL nucleus contained close to 40% of the retrogradely labeled cells expressing Fos protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Photoinhibition of the AM>ACA projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear response.
source: Our results showed that photoinhibition of the AM>ACA projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear response and impaired the acquisition of contextual fear response to a predator threat (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the AM>ACA projection impaired the acquisition of contextual fear response to a predator threat.
source: Our results showed that photoinhibition of the AM>ACA projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear response and impaired the acquisition of contextual fear response to a predator threat (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>BLA projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear responses.
source: Our results showed that photoinhibition of the ACA>BLA projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear responses reducing risk assessment and increasing exploration compared to the control group (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>BLA projection in eNpHR3.0-expressing mice during predatory context did not change the risk assessment and exploration times compared to the control group.
source: Conversely, photoinhibition of the ACA>BLA projection in eNpHR3.0-expressing mice during predatory context did not change the risk assessment and exploration times compared to the control group (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>BLA projection impairs the acquisition but not the expression of contextual fear response to a predator threat.
source: The results suggest that photoinhibition of the ACA>BLA projection impairs the acquisition but not the expression of contextual fear response to a predator threat.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of ACA>BLA pathway silencing during acquisition but not expression phases.

claim: The ACA contained a significantly larger percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in animals exposed to the cat (83.2%) compared to those exposed to the predatory context (24%).
source: The ACA contained a significantly larger percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in animals exposed to the cat (83.2%, double-to-chance ratio=1.94, 95%confidence interval [CI] [1.42, 2.47]) compared to those exposed to the predatory context (24%, double-to-chance ratio=0.81, 95% CI [0.61, 1.02]) (Figure 5E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 5E and G with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a larger engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the BLA during the acquisition compared to the expression of contextual fear anti-predatory responses.
source: This suggests a larger engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the BLA during the acquisition compared to the expression of contextual fear anti-predatory responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional tracing data showing differential activation patterns.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>PERI projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear responses.
source: The results showed that photoinhibition of the ACA>PERI projection during cat exposure did not change innate fear responses but significantly reduced contextual fear responses reducing risk assessment and increasing exploration compared to the control group (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>PERI projection in eNpHR3.0-expressing mice during predatory context did not change the risk assessment and exploration times versus the control group.
source: Conversely, photoinhibition of the ACA>PERI projection in eNpHR3.0-expressing mice during predatory context did not change the risk assessment and exploration times versus the control group (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6F showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Silencing the ACA>PERI projection impairs the acquisition but not the expression of contextual fear response to a predator threat.
source: The results suggest that silencing the ACA>PERI projection impairs the acquisition but not the expression of contextual fear response to a predator threat.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of ACA>PERI pathway silencing during acquisition but not expression phases.

claim: The ACA contained a significantly larger percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in animals exposed to the cat (48.5%) compared to those exposed to the predatory context (15.2%) for the PERI projection.
source: here, the ACA contained a significantly larger percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in animals exposed to the cat (48.5%, double-to-chance ratio=1.10, 95% CI [0.84, 1.37]) compared to those exposed to the predatory context (15.2%, double-to-chance ratio=0.64 95% CI [0.53, 0.75]) (Figure 6E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 6E and G with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a larger engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the PERI during the acquisition compared to the expression of contextual fear responses.
source: This suggests a larger engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the PERI during the acquisition compared to the expression of contextual fear responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional tracing data showing differential activation patterns.

claim: NpHR3.0-expressing mice that received photoinhibition of the ACA>POST projection during cat exposure or predatory context did not change the risk assessment responses and fearless exploration.
source: Compared to the control group, NpHR3.0-expressing mice that received photoinhibition of the ACA>POST projection during cat exposure or predatory context did not change the risk assessment responses and fearless exploration during exposure to the environment previously visited by a predator (Figure 7D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7D and F showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Silencing the ACA>POST projection apparently had no effect on the acquisition and expression of contextual fear to a predator threat.
source: The results suggest that silencing the ACA>POST projection apparently had no effect on the acquisition and expression of contextual fear to a predator threat.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing no effects of ACA>POST pathway silencing.

claim: The ACA contained a relatively low percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in response either to the cat (21.4%) or the predatory context (19.1%) for the POST projection.
source: Functional tracing in POST FG-injected animals revealed that the ACA contained a relatively low percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in response either to the cat (21.4%, double-to-chance ratio = 0.52 95% CI [0.38, 0.65]) or the predatory context (19.1%, double-to-chance ratio = 0.78 95% CI [0.68, 0.88]) (Figure 7E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 7E and G with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a relatively small engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the POST during both the acquisition and expression of contextual fear anti-predatory responses.
source: Thus, there is a relatively small engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the POST during both the acquisition and expression of contextual fear anti-predatory responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional tracing data showing low activation patterns.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>PAGdl projection during cat exposure did not change innate or contextual fear responses.
source: These results revealed that photoinhibition of the ACA>PAGdl projection during cat exposure did not change innate or contextual fear responses (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8D showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>PAGdl projection during exposure to the predatory context in eNpHR3.0-expressing mice yielded a significant decrease in the risk assessment and an increase in exploration.
source: Conversely, compared to the control group, photoinhibition of the ACA>PAGdl projection during exposure to the predatory context in eNpHR3.0-expressing mice yielded a significant decrease in the risk assessment and an increase in exploration (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8F showing behavioral measurements.

claim: Photoinhibition of the ACA>PAGdl projection had no effect on the acquisition but impaired the expression of contextual fear to a predator threat.
source: The results showed that photoinhibition of the ACA>PAGdl projection had no effect on the acquisition but impaired the expression of contextual fear to a predator threat.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of ACA>PAGdl pathway silencing during expression but not acquisition phases.

claim: The ACA contained a significantly larger percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in animals exposed to the predatory context (75.2%) compared to those exposed to the cat (29.9%) for the PAGdl projection.
source: The ACA contained a significantly larger percentage of double-labeled Fos/FG cells in animals exposed to the predatory context (75.2%, double-to-chance ratio=2.66 95% CI [2.30, 3.02]) compared to those exposed to the cat (29.9%, double-to-chance ratio = 0.67 95% CI [0.43, 0.90]) (Figure 8E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional tracing data presented in Figure 8E and G with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a larger engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the PAGdl during the expression compared to the acquisition of contextual fear responses.
source: This suggests a larger engagement of the ACA cells projecting to the PAGdl during the expression compared to the acquisition of contextual fear responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional tracing data showing differential activation patterns.

claim: During cat exposure, rats spend close to 90% of the time freezing and 2% of the time risk assessing the environment.
source: Notably, the defensive responses in mice differ somewhat from those seen in rats exposed to cats and then to the predator-associated context. During cat exposure, rats spend close to 90% of the time freezing and 2% of the time risk assessing the environment Ribeiro-Barbosa et al., 2005
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ribeiro-Barbosa et al., 2005 study.

claim: Mice froze for approximately 30% of the time and risk assessed the environment for close to 30% of the time during cat exposure.
source: mice froze for approximately 30% of the time and risk assessed the environment for close to 30% of the time (see Appendix – Behavioral Protocol).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the Appendix.

claim: During exposure to the predatory context, rats only froze a little and then spent time risk assessing the predator-related context for 70% of the time.
source: During exposure to the predatory context, rats only froze a little and then spent time risk assessing the predator-related context for 70% of the time (Ribeiro-Barbosa et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ribeiro-Barbosa et al., 2005 study.

claim: Mice presented no freezing and a relatively weaker risk assessment response—close to 50% of the time during exposure to the predatory context.
source: which is different from mice that presented no freezing and a relatively weaker risk assessment response—close to 50% of the time (see Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: ACA Fos expression in response to the cat and cat-related context was significantly higher relative to its expression level in response to exposure to a novel non-threat stimulus and to the context paired with a non-threat stimulus.
source: This analysis revealed that ACA Fos expression in response to the cat and cat-related context was significantly higher relative to its expression level in response to exposure to a novel non-threat stimulus and to the context paired with a non-threat stimulus (see Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The retrosplenial cortex is critical for the recognition of an environment directly paired with an aversive event.
source: The retrosplenial cortex is critical for the recognition of an environment directly paired with an aversive event (Robinson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Robinson et al., 2018 study.

claim: Landmark cues served as dominant reference points and anchored in the retrosplenial cortex the spatial code, which is the result of local integration of visual, motor, and spatial information.
source: Recent studies using two-photon imaging revealed that landmark cues served as dominant reference points and anchored in the retrosplenial cortex the spatial code, which is the result of local integration of visual, motor, and spatial information (Fischer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2020 study.

claim: The VISm is necessary for the visuospatial discrimination used in the integration of allocentric visuospatial cues.
source: The VISm is necessary for the visuospatial discrimination used in the integration of allocentric visuospatial cues (Sánchez et al., 1997; Espinoza et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sánchez et al., 1997 and Espinoza et al., 1999 studies.

claim: The CL receives projections from the dorsal part of the periaqueductal gray.
source: The CL receives projections from the dorsal part of the periaqueductal gray (Kincheski et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kincheski et al., 2012 study.

claim: The AMv receives substantial inputs from the dorsal premammillary nucleus.
source: the AMv receives substantial inputs from the dorsal premammillary nucleus (Canteras and Swanson, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Canteras and Swanson, 1992 study.

claim: The dorsal premammillary nucleus is part of the predator-responsive circuit of the medial hypothalamus.
source: The dorsal premammillary nucleus is part of the predator-responsive circuit of the medial hypothalamus (Gross and Canteras, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gross and Canteras, 2012 study.

claim: The dorsal premammillary nucleus is the most responsive site to a live predator or its odor.
source: and is the most responsive site to a live predator or its odor (Cezario et al., 2008; Dielenberg et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cezario et al., 2008 and Dielenberg et al., 2001 studies.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the AM drastically reduced the acquisition but not the expression of contextual fear responses to predator threats.
source: In line with this result, studies from our group have shown that pharmacological inactivation of the AM drastically reduced the acquisition but not the expression of contextual fear responses to predator threats (de Lima et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to de Lima et al., 2017 study.

claim: Anterior thalamic lesions slow down the acquisition of contextual fear conditioning but do not affect contextual fear memory tested in the short term.
source: It is noteworthy that anterior thalamic lesions slow down the acquisition of contextual fear conditioning but do not affect contextual fear memory tested in the short term (Dupire et al., 2013; Marchand et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dupire et al., 2013 and Marchand et al., 2014 studies.

claim: Ventral hippocampal cytotoxic lesions significantly reduced conditioned defensive behaviors during re-exposure to the predator-associated context.
source: Ventral hippocampal cytotoxic lesions significantly reduced conditioned defensive behaviors during re-exposure to the predator-associated context (Pentkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pentkowski et al., 2006 study.

claim: Cytotoxic NMDA lesions in the BLA impaired contextual fear responses to predator threat.
source: Likewise, cytotoxic NMDA lesions in the BLA impaired contextual fear responses to predator threat (Martinez et al., 2011; Bindi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martinez et al., 2011 and Bindi et al., 2018 studies.

claim: The PERI provides dense projections to the BLA and the hippocampal formation.
source: Tract-tracing studies revealed that the PERI provides dense projections to the BLA and the hippocampal formation (Shi and Cassell, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shi and Cassell, 1999 study.

claim: Close to 50% of ACA cells projecting to the BLA and PERI provided a branched projection to both targets.
source: Triple retrograde tracing experiments revealed that the ACA cells projecting to the BLA and the PERI were mostly found in the supragranular layers (layers II and III), and close to 50% of these cells provided a branched projection to the BLA and PERI (see in the Appendix, Triple retrograde tracing and Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple retrograde tracing presented in Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: The POST is necessary for normal acquisition of contextual and auditory fear conditioning.
source: The POST in turn is necessary for normal acquisition of contextual and auditory fear conditioning (Robinson and Bucci, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Robinson and Bucci, 2012 study.

claim: Exposure to the predatory context yields a significant Fos expression in the dorsal PAG.
source: Exposure to the predatory context yields a significant Fos expression in the dorsal PAG (Cezario et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cezario et al., 2008 study.

claim: Electrical, pharmacological, and optogenetic stimulation of the dorsal PAG have been shown to produce freezing, flight, and risk assessment behavior in the absence of a predatory threat.
source: a region where electrical, pharmacological, and optogenetic stimulation have been shown to produce freezing, flight, and risk assessment behavior in the absence of a predatory threat (Bittencourt et al., 2004; Assareh et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bittencourt et al., 2004, Assareh et al., 2016, and Deng et al., 2016 studies.

claim: ACA cells projecting to the PAGdl are in the infragranular layers (layers V and VI) and do not overlap with the cells projecting to the BLA or PERI.
source: Triple retrograde tracing experiments revealed that ACA cells projecting to the PAGdl are in the infragranular layers (layers V and VI) and do not overlap with the cells projecting to the BLA or PERI (see in the Appendix, Triple retrograde tracing and Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple retrograde tracing presented in Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: The ACA can provide predictive relationships between the context and the predator threat and influences fear memory acquisition through projections to the BLA and PERI and the expression of contextual fear through projections to the PAGdl.
source: Overall, the ACA can provide predictive relationships between the context and the predator threat and influences fear memory acquisition through projections to the BLA and PERI and the expression of contextual fear through projections to the PAGdl.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both the predator- and conspecific-responsive hypothalamic circuits comprise the dorsal premammillary nucleus that projects densely to the AMv nucleus.
source: Notably, both the predator- and conspecific-responsive hypothalamic circuits comprise the dorsal premammillary nucleus that projects densely to the AMv nucleus (Canteras and Swanson, 1992), and therefore, engage the AMv>ACA pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Canteras and Swanson, 1992 study.

claim: The anteromedial thalamus' cytotoxic lesions impair contextual fear in a social defeat-associated context.
source: Of relevance, previous studies showed that the anteromedial thalamus' cytotoxic lesions impair contextual fear in a social defeat-associated context (Rangel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rangel et al., 2018 study.

claim: Male and female mice present similar defensive responses during exposure to the predator or predatory context.
source: We observed that male and female mice present similar defensive responses during exposure to the predator or predatory context (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: A recent study carried out in male and female mice examining the role of the dorsal premammillary nucleus on coordination of anti-predatory responses did not report differences between sexes.
source: A recent study carried out in male and female mice examining the role of the dorsal premammillary nucleus—a key element of the hypothalamic predator-responsive circuit—on coordination of anti-predatory responses did not report differences between sexes (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021 study.

claim: Critical sites in defensive circuits, such as the hypothalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala, are responsive to gonadal steroid hormones.
source: However, sex differences are expected in terms of the responsivity of elements of defensive circuits, especially considering that critical sites in these circuits, such as the hypothalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala, are responsive to gonadal steroid hormones (Simerly et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Simerly et al., 1990 study.

claim: Patch-clamp experiments showed that transfected neurons (Gi-DREADD neurons) were hyperpolarized as they underwent extracellular CNO and presented a significant decrease in the triggering of action potentials after 10 µM CNO.
source: Patch-clamp experiments showed that transfected neurons (Gi-DREADD neurons) were hyperpolarized as they underwent extracellular CNO and presented a significant decrease in the triggering of action potentials (APs) after 10 µM CNO (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Patch-clamp experiments in neurons transfected with halorhodopsin revealed a robust hyperpolarization with 585 nm light on with clear linear regression due to different light intensities.
source: To test the efficiency of light-induced hyperpolarization in eNpHR3.0-expressing neurons, the patch-clamp experiments in neurons transfected with halorhodopsin revealed a robust hyperpolarization with 585 nm light on with clear linear regression due to different light intensities (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Patch-clamp experiments showed clear inhibition of EPSC of postsynaptic cells after illumination at 585 nm on halorhodopsin-positive fibers and no rebound excitation following halorhodopsin activation.
source: Moreover, patch-clamp experiments tested the efficiency of pre-synaptic inhibitions and showed clear inhibition of EPSC of postsynaptic cells after illumination at 585 nm on halorhodopsin-positive fibers and no rebound excitation following halorhodopsin activation (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The ACA is involved in both the acquisition and expression of contextual fear to predatory threat.
source: The experiments were made in mice and revealed that the ACA is involved in both the acquisition and expression of contextual fear to predatory threat.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ACA occupies a pivotal position in a cortical network responsive to predatory threats.
source: The anterior cingulate area (ACA) occupies a pivotal position in a cortical network responsive to predatory threats, and it exerts a critical role in processing fear memory.
evidence: The claim is based on the anatomical and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ACA exerts a critical role in processing fear memory.
source: The anterior cingulate area (ACA) occupies a pivotal position in a cortical network responsive to predatory threats, and it exerts a critical role in processing fear memory.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ACA integrates contextual and predator cues during the acquisition phase to provide predictive relationships between the context and the threatening stimuli and influence memory storage.
source: Our findings collectively support the idea that the ACA integrates contextual and predator cues during the acquisition phase to provide predictive relationships between the context and the threatening stimuli and influence memory storage.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ventral hippocampus and BLA appear as critical sites for memory storage of contextual fear to predator threats.
source: The ventral hippocampus and BLA appear as critical sites for memory storage of contextual fear to predator threats.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature and experimental data.

claim: Cycloheximide injection in the BLA or the ventral hippocampus impairs contextual fear responses to predatory threat.
source: In line with these ideas, recent findings from our lab indicate that cycloheximide (a protein synthesis inhibitor) injection in the BLA or the ventral hippocampus impairs contextual fear responses to predatory threat (F. Reis and N.S. Canteras personal observations).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished personal observations mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: The prefrontal cortex is likely to influence memory storage in the amygdala and hippocampus using two branches: one direct branch to the BLA and another branch to the perirhinal cortices.
source: Previous model of the prefrontal regulation of memory formation suggests that the prefrontal cortex is likely to influence memory storage in the amygdala and hippocampus using two branches (Gilmartin et al., 2014). One direct branch is to the BLA and conveys information about the predictive value of the relevant clues during learning. The other branch is to the perirhinal cortices, which occupies a strategic position in this network influencing both the hippocampus and the amygdala.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gilmartin et al., 2014 study.

claim: The continuous yellow laser stimulation did not produce tissue damage in the soundings of the optic fiber tips.
source: Note that the continuous yellow laser stimulation did not produce tissue damage in the soundings of the optic fiber tips (see Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data presented in Appendix 1—figure 11.
